questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of an efficient respiratory surface?
questions.explanation: Gases must dissolve and then diffuse across the surface, so anything thick or waterproof is a barrier. Efficient surfaces are instead thin, moist, extensive and well supplied with blood to keep the concentration gradient steep.

distractorRationale.a: A large area allows more molecules to diffuse per unit time
distractorRationale.c: Oxygen and carbon dioxide must dissolve before crossing the membrane
distractorRationale.d: Blood flow removes absorbed gas and maintains the diffusion gradient

questions.stem: The respiratory organ of a grasshopper is the
questions.explanation: Insects have a branching network of air tubes called tracheae that open to the outside through spiracles along the body. The finest branches carry air directly to the tissues, so insect blood plays almost no part in oxygen transport.

distractorRationale.a: Gills are used by aquatic animals such as fish and tadpoles
distractorRationale.b: Lungs are found in mammals, birds, reptiles and adult amphibians
distractorRationale.d: Moist skin is the surface used by earthworms and, partly, by toads

questions.stem: An earthworm placed on dry sand in the sun soon dies. The best biological explanation is that

options.text: the sand is too heavy for it to burrow through
its skin dries out, so oxygen can no longer dissolve and diffuse into the blood
it cannot find food on sand

questions.explanation: An earthworm has no lungs or gills and exchanges gases entirely through its skin. Oxygen must first dissolve in the film of moisture on that skin before it can diffuse into the capillaries beneath, so once the skin dries the worm suffocates.

distractorRationale.a: Death follows within minutes, far too quickly to be a burrowing problem
distractorRationale.c: Starvation would take days, not minutes
distractorRationale.d: Sunlight is harmful mainly through drying, not by destroying nerves

questions.stem: During inspiration in humans, which set of events occurs?

options.text: The diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards, and thoracic volume decreases
The diaphragm contracts and flattens, thoracic volume increases and pressure falls
The lung muscles contract to pull air inwards
The ribs move downwards and inwards while pressure rises

questions.explanation: The diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, so the chest cavity expands both downwards and outwards. The larger volume lowers the pressure inside the thorax below atmospheric pressure, and air flows in until the two are equal.

distractorRationale.a: This describes expiration, when the diaphragm relaxes
distractorRationale.c: Lung tissue contains no muscle at all; the lungs are inflated passively
distractorRationale.d: Downward rib movement and rising pressure occur during expiration

questions.stem: Which gas is present in almost exactly the same proportion in inspired and expired air?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 79% of both inspired and expired air because the body neither uses it nor produces it. Oxygen falls from about 21% to 16%, carbon dioxide rises from about 0.04% to 4%, and expired air is saturated with water vapour.

distractorRationale.a: Oxygen is used in respiration, so it falls by about a quarter
distractorRationale.b: Carbon dioxide is produced by respiration, so it rises about a hundredfold
distractorRationale.d: Expired air is saturated with water vapour, usually far more than inspired air

questions.stem: Amoeba has no special respiratory organ while a goat has lungs with millions of alveoli. The reason is that as an organism becomes larger, its

options.text: surface area to volume ratio decreases, so its outer surface alone cannot supply enough oxygen
surface area to volume ratio increases, so it needs less surface
skin becomes more permeable to gases

questions.explanation: Volume rises with the cube of length while surface area rises only with the square, so a large animal has proportionally far less surface per unit of living tissue. Highly folded internal organs such as alveoli restore the area needed, and a blood system carries the gases the last short distance to each cell.

distractorRationale.b: The ratio falls with increasing size, which is the whole problem
distractorRationale.c: Every living cell needs oxygen for aerobic respiration, whatever the size of the animal
distractorRationale.d: Land animals have less permeable skin, to reduce water loss

questions.stem: The trachea is supported by C-shaped rings of cartilage. These rings

options.text: keep the airway open and prevent it collapsing when pressure inside falls
carry out gaseous exchange with the blood

questions.explanation: Inspiration works by lowering the pressure inside the airway, which would tend to squeeze a soft tube shut. The cartilage rings hold the trachea permanently open, and the gap in each C allows the oesophagus behind it to expand when food is swallowed.

distractorRationale.a: Mucus is secreted by goblet cells in the lining, not by cartilage
distractorRationale.c: Air is warmed mainly in the nasal cavity
distractorRationale.d: Exchange occurs only in the alveoli, whose walls are one cell thick

questions.stem: The lungs inflate because muscles in the lung tissue itself contract and pull air inwards.
questions.explanation: False. Lung tissue is elastic but contains no muscle. The diaphragm and intercostal muscles change the volume of the thoracic cavity, and the resulting pressure difference moves air in and out while the lungs follow passively.

questions.stem: A toad can survive submerged in a pond for a long period without surfacing because it

options.text: has gills throughout its adult life
can exchange gases through its moist skin as well as through its lungs
stores enough oxygen in its bladder

questions.explanation: Adult amphibians use three surfaces: lungs, the lining of the mouth, and the thin moist skin, which is richly supplied with capillaries. Under water the skin alone can meet the modest oxygen demand of a resting toad.

distractorRationale.a: Gills are present only in the tadpole stage and are lost at metamorphosis
distractorRationale.c: Respiration in cells never stops in a living animal
distractorRationale.d: The bladder stores urine, not oxygen

questions.stem: State four features of an efficient respiratory surface and explain how the alveoli of a human lung show each of them.
markingGuide: Feature 1 — large surface area: about 700 million alveoli give a combined area of roughly 70 square metres in a small volume (2 marks)
Feature 2 — thin surface: each alveolar wall is one cell thick and lies against a capillary wall also one cell thick, so oxygen crosses only two cell layers (2 marks)
Feature 3 — moist surface: the alveolar lining is covered by a film of fluid in which oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve before diffusing (2 marks)
Feature 4 — rich blood supply: a dense capillary network continually removes oxygenated blood and delivers deoxygenated blood, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient (2 marks)
Accept also ventilation by breathing, which replaces the air in the alveoli and keeps the gradient steep (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Each general feature must be tied to a specific measurable property of the alveolus rather than merely restated. The strongest answers also mention that ventilation and blood flow work together to keep the concentration gradient steep, since diffusion would otherwise slow to a halt.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of an efficient respiratory surface?

options.text: It has a large surface area.
It is located deep in the body.

questions.explanation: An efficient respiratory surface must have a large surface area to allow for maximum gas exchange. This feature is essential for organisms to efficiently take in oxygen and expel carbon dioxide.

distractorRationale.a: Thick and dry surfaces would hinder gas exchange.
distractorRationale.c: An impermeable surface would prevent gas exchange altogether.
distractorRationale.d: Being deep in the body would limit exposure to the environment.

questions.stem: What is the primary respiratory organ in humans?
questions.explanation: Humans primarily use lungs for respiration, which are specialized organs designed for gas exchange. They allow for the intake of oxygen and the release of carbon dioxide.

distractorRationale.a: Skin respiration is not sufficient for humans.
distractorRationale.b: Gills are used by aquatic organisms, not humans.
distractorRationale.d: The trachea is a passageway to the lungs, not a respiratory organ.

distractorRationale.a: Frogs use lungs as adults, although they have gills in their tadpole stage.
distractorRationale.c: Humans rely on lungs for respiration.
distractorRationale.d: Lizards also use lungs for breathing.

questions.stem: What mechanism is primarily responsible for the process of expiration in humans?
questions.explanation: During expiration, the diaphragm relaxes, which reduces the volume of the thoracic cavity and pushes air out of the lungs. This process is crucial for breathing.

distractorRationale.a: Contraction of the diaphragm occurs during inspiration.
distractorRationale.c: Expansion of the rib cage occurs during inspiration.
distractorRationale.d: Increased lung volume is associated with inhalation, not exhalation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a respiratory surface in living organisms?
questions.explanation: The heart is not a respiratory surface; it is an organ that pumps blood throughout the body. Respiratory surfaces facilitate gas exchange, while the heart's function is circulation.

distractorRationale.a: Lungs are a primary respiratory organ in mammals.
distractorRationale.b: Skin can serve as a respiratory surface in some organisms.
distractorRationale.c: Stomata are openings in plants that facilitate gas exchange.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the alveoli in human lungs?
questions.explanation: Alveoli are tiny air sacs in the lungs that provide a large surface area for gas exchange, allowing oxygen to enter the blood and carbon dioxide to be expelled.

distractorRationale.a: Mucus is produced by goblet cells, not alveoli.
distractorRationale.c: Oxygen is transported by red blood cells, not the alveoli.
distractorRationale.d: Air is filtered primarily by the nasal passages and bronchi.

questions.stem: In which phase of breathing does the diaphragm contract?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, increasing the thoracic cavity's volume and allowing air to flow into the lungs.

distractorRationale.a: Expiration involves the relaxation of the diaphragm.
distractorRationale.c: The resting phase does not involve active contraction.
distractorRationale.d: Hyperventilation is an increased rate of breathing but does not specify diaphragm movement.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the respiratory system is TRUE?

options.text: Gas exchange occurs in the trachea.
The alveoli are surrounded by capillaries.
The diaphragm is a voluntary muscle.

questions.explanation: Alveoli are small air sacs in the lungs that are surrounded by capillaries, where the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide takes place. This structure is crucial for efficient respiration.

distractorRationale.a: Gas exchange does not occur in the trachea; it occurs in the alveoli.
distractorRationale.c: The diaphragm is an involuntary muscle that controls breathing.
distractorRationale.d: Breathing occurs continuously, not just during exercise.

questions.stem: Which gas is primarily exchanged in the alveoli?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is the primary gas exchanged in the alveoli during respiration. It diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, while carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli to be exhaled.

distractorRationale.a: Nitrogen is not actively exchanged; it remains relatively constant.
distractorRationale.c: Carbon monoxide is not a primary gas involved in respiration.
distractorRationale.d: Hydrogen is not a significant gas in the respiratory process.

questions.stem: What is the role of surfactant in the alveoli?
questions.explanation: Surfactant reduces surface tension in the alveoli, preventing them from collapsing and ensuring efficient gas exchange. It plays a critical role in maintaining lung stability.

distractorRationale.a: Increasing surface tension would make it difficult for the alveoli to function.
distractorRationale.c: While surfactant helps with lung function, trapping pathogens is not its primary role.
distractorRationale.d: Surfactant does not absorb oxygen; its function is related to surface tension.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the process of inhalation?

options.text: Air is pushed out of the lungs.
The diaphragm relaxes and air enters.
The diaphragm contracts and air enters.
The rib cage decreases in volume.

questions.explanation: Inhalation occurs when the diaphragm contracts, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity, which causes air to flow into the lungs. This is a key part of the breathing process.

distractorRationale.a: This describes exhalation, not inhalation.
distractorRationale.b: The diaphragm must contract for inhalation, not relax.
distractorRationale.d: The rib cage expands during inhalation, not decreases.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms utilizes skin as a respiratory surface?

distractorRationale.b: Fish primarily use gills for respiration, not skin.
distractorRationale.c: Humans use lungs for respiration, not skin.
distractorRationale.d: Birds have specialized lungs and air sacs for respiration.

questions.stem: What is the primary function of the alveoli in the lungs?
questions.explanation: The primary function of the alveoli is to facilitate gas exchange between the air and the blood. They provide a large surface area for oxygen to enter the bloodstream and carbon dioxide to be expelled.

distractorRationale.a: Mucus production is a function of goblet cells, not alveoli.
distractorRationale.c: Oxygen is transported by red blood cells after gas exchange occurs in the alveoli.
distractorRationale.d: Air filtration occurs mainly in the nasal passages and trachea, not in the alveoli.

distractorRationale.c: Cartilage rings support the trachea but do not directly affect alveoli.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the process of external respiration?

options.text: Gas exchange between blood and tissues
Gas exchange between air and blood
Transport of gases in the bloodstream

questions.explanation: External respiration refers to the exchange of gases between the air in the alveoli and the blood in the pulmonary capillaries, primarily involving the intake of oxygen and the release of carbon dioxide.

distractorRationale.a: That describes internal respiration, not external respiration.
distractorRationale.c: Energy production in cells is related to cellular respiration, not external respiration.
distractorRationale.d: Gas transport occurs after external respiration has taken place.
